statement: Omar has 26 minutes left for ten 5-point questions. Reading all ten first takes 3 minutes. He learns they would take him 8, 3, 11, 5, 9, 4, 12, 6, 10 and 7 minutes to solve correctly. A random guess takes no time and is worth 1 point on average. What is his largest expected score from these ten?

choices.misconception: I chose the four quickest questions correctly but left the other six blank instead of guessing, losing the 6 points the guesses are worth on average.
I worked through the questions in printed order, 8, 3 and 11 minutes, until time ran out, so I solved only three and guessed seven.
I forgot the 3 minutes of reading, so I fitted five questions into 26 minutes, and then I also forgot to guess on the other five.
I forgot to take off the 3 minutes of reading, so I fitted five questions, 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 25 minutes, into the time and guessed the other five.

hints: After reading, how many minutes are really left for solving?
With 23 minutes, solving the quickest questions first fits in the most. Every question you do not solve should still be answered, because a guess is worth something on average.
The quickest take 3, 4, 5 and 6 minutes, 18 in all; adding the 7-minute one would need 25. So four are solved for 20 points and six are guessed for about 6 points.

solutions.reliable: Reading uses 3 of the 26 minutes, leaving 23. Every solved question is worth the same 5 points, so he should solve as many as possible, quickest first: $3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 18$ minutes, while adding the next one (7 minutes) would need 25 > 23. So the most he can solve is four, for 20 points. The other six are guessed, worth $6 \times 1 = 6$ points on average. Total: 26. The transferable idea: in the 5-point block, read everything first, take the quickest wins, and never leave a blank.

whyOnTest: The 5-point block rewards reading all of it first, choosing the quickest wins and guessing the rest; each step you skip costs points here.
